title: food as practice
hook: a knock at the door just as dinner is served: the Upanishad says to make much food for exactly this

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice meant the Gita's three kinds of food, sorted by what they do to the eater, and the test of the hour after.

Dinner is on the table, exactly enough for the people sitting at it, counted out, served. And then a knock at the door. A cousin passing through, a neighbor, a friend of a friend who's hungry and a little embarrassed about the timing. Everyone at the table does the same quick arithmetic. The Taittiriya Upanishad, the same text where Bhrigu found food, has already thought about this knock, and its answer comes before the knock does. Today, food that doesn't stop at your own plate.
screen: `DINNER, COUNTED OUT.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `THE ANSWER COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Near the end of Bhrigu's story, the Upanishad gives this rule, paraphrased: do not turn away anyone who comes to your dwelling for shelter. And so, it says, gather much food, so there is food to give. That's the answer to the knock. Not a quick calculation at the door, but a kitchen that cooks, from the start, for more than the people already sitting down. Earlier, in its teaching to departing students, the same Upanishad says, in Sanskrit, atithi devo bhava: let the guest be a god to you. The guest isn't a disruption to the meal; the guest is honored at it like a god. The Bhagavad Gita says it from the other side. Krishna says, paraphrased, that good people who eat what remains after the offering are freed from their faults, but those who cook only for their own sake eat their own wrong. This lands in three places. First, it reframes these food days. Measure, attention, the hour after: all of that could stay private. These verses won't let it. Food as practice is also food as hospitality. Second, the order matters: offer first, eat what remains. In some Hindu homes a first portion is set aside before the family eats, for a guest, for a cow, for the birds. Third, it's practical. Make a little more. Keep a spare plate. The rule isn't a feeling about generosity; it's a way of cooking, decided before anyone knocks.
screen: `TURN NO ONE AWAY` · `LET THE GUEST BE A GOD TO YOU` · `COOKING ONLY FOR YOURSELF` · `A FIRST PORTION SET ASIDE`

segments.voice: Picture the place where you usually eat, add one more seat, and let a face come for it: a friend you haven't fed in a while, a neighbor, someone alone. Hold that face kindly with the breath, or if no one comes, hold the empty seat itself, open. If you pray, hold that person in prayer.
Food as practice. In the Upanishad: turn no one away, and make much food; let the guest be a god to you. Food that doesn't stop at your own plate. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. A kitchen that cooks for one more is ready for the knock. Back tomorrow, same hill.

chat.says: Why do your parents always cook way more than we can eat?
options: The Upanishad says turn no one away and make much food, so there's always some to give.
The Upanishad says a big pot keeps food warm longer, so cooking extra is just practical.
The Upanishad says a full pot shows wealth, so cooking big is about looking generous.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.10 (do not turn away anyone who comes for shelter; therefore gather much food)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (the teacher's instruction to departing students: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you)
Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (the good who eat the remains of the offering are freed from faults; those who cook for their own sake eat sin)

notes: Taittiriya 3.10: confirm the paraphrase 'do not turn away anyone who comes to your dwelling for shelter; therefore one should gather much food'. 'Near the end of Bhrigu's story' places it in the Bhriguvalli (third section).

Taittiriya 1.11: confirm it is addressed to departing students (the convocation teaching) and the gloss of atithi devo bhava. Atithi was used on earlier days (e.g. 51, 86, 390–391, 972–973); this day ties it to food as practice.
Gita 3.13: 'freed from their faults' and 'eat their own wrong' paraphrase 'freed from all sins' and 'eat sin'; confirm.
'In some Hindu homes a first portion is set aside ... for a guest, for a cow, for the birds' (go-grasa, the bali offerings): confirm wording.
This day leans on the Upanishads and the Gita more than Ayurveda; the part title is 'Ayurveda as a lens'. Flag if a Keeper wants an Ayurvedic source added.
